chunks: [1] Mu‘āwiyah is not more cunning than I am, but he deceives and commits evil deeds. Had it not been for the reprehensibility of deceit, I would have been the most cunning of all men. But (the fact is that) every deceit is a sin and every sin is disobedience (of Allāh), and every deceitful person will have a banner by which he will be recognised on the Day of Judgement.
By Allāh, I cannot be made forgetful by strategy, nor can I be overpowered by hardships.
ai.seo_question: How does Imam Ali distinguish his own cunning from Muawiya's in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In this famous declaration, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) distinguishes between political cunning (khada') and moral integrity, asserting that his restraint from treachery is a conscious ethical choice rather than an inability. He establishes a theological chain linking deceit (ghadr) to sin (fujur) and disbelief (kufr), promising that every traitor will carry a unique banner on the Day of Judgment, a concept deeply rooted in Shia exegetical tradition regarding the signs of the hypocrites. This statement serves as a critique of Mu'awiya’s pragmatic politics, framing his rule not just as a political contest but as a spiritual deviation marked by the 'banner of treachery.'
